u:iv-46-100-doors.title: 100 doors
u:iv-46-100-doors.summary: Only perfect-square doors stay open — because they have an odd number of divisors.

blocks.text: **Puzzle**: 100 doors, all closed. In pass i (i = 1..100), you toggle every i-th door. Which doors are open at the end?
A door n is toggled once for each **divisor** of n. It ends **open** if toggled an **odd** number of times — i.e. if n has an odd number of divisors.

Divisors come in pairs (d and n/d), so most numbers have an even count — EXCEPT **perfect squares**, where one divisor (the square root) pairs with itself, giving an odd count. So the open doors are the perfect squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100 — exactly **10** doors.
The general answer for N doors: floor(sqrt(N)) doors remain open.

mcqs.q: After all 100 passes, which doors are open?
mcqs.explain: A door ends open iff it has an odd number of divisors, which only perfect squares do.

mcqs.q: How many doors remain open out of 100?
mcqs.explain: There are 10 perfect squares from 1 to 100.

mcqs.q: Perfect squares have an odd number of divisors because:
options: The square root divisor pairs with itself, not another divisor
mcqs.explain: Divisors pair as (d, n/d); for a perfect square the root pairs with itself, making the count odd.

u:iv-47-25-horses-5-tracks.title: 25 horses, 5 tracks
u:iv-47-25-horses-5-tracks.summary: Find the top 3 fastest of 25 horses in a minimum of 7 races (5 at a time, no timer).

blocks.text: **Puzzle**: 25 horses, a track that races 5 at a time, no stopwatch (only relative order). Minimum races to find the top 3?

items: **5 races** — split into 5 groups of 5; race each. (5 races so far.)
**Race 6** — race the 5 group-winners. This ranks the winners; the overall 1st is the fastest horse.
**Eliminate**: only horses that could be top-3 remain — from the winners' race, the 4th and 5th groups are out entirely, and within groups only certain horses can still place.
**Race 7** — race the ~5 remaining candidates for 2nd and 3rd (1st is already known). Total: **7 races**.

blocks.text: The answer is **7**. The trick: after ranking group winners (race 6), you can eliminate horses that are provably not top-3 (they lost to at least 3 faster horses), leaving exactly enough candidates for one final race to decide 2nd and 3rd.

mcqs.q: The minimum number of races to find the top 3 of 25 horses (5 at a time, no timer) is:
mcqs.explain: 5 group races + 1 race of winners + 1 final race of remaining candidates = 7.

mcqs.q: After racing the 5 group winners, the overall fastest horse is:
options: The winner of the winners' race
mcqs.explain: The winner of the winners' race beat all other group winners, so it's the fastest of all 25.

mcqs.q: The elimination step works because a horse can't be top-3 if it:
options: Lost to at least 3 horses known to be faster
mcqs.explain: Any horse behind 3 provably-faster horses cannot be in the top 3, so it's eliminated.

u:iv-48-3-bulbs-3-switches.title: 3 bulbs, 3 switches
u:iv-48-3-bulbs-3-switches.summary: Identify which switch controls which bulb in one visit — use heat.

blocks.text: **Puzzle**: 3 switches outside a room, 3 bulbs inside. You can flip switches freely but may enter the room **only once**. Which switch controls which bulb?

items: Turn on **switch 1**, wait a few minutes, then turn it **off**.
Turn on **switch 2** and leave it on.
Enter the room once.

blocks.text: Inside: the bulb that is **ON** is switch 2. The bulb that is **OFF but WARM** is switch 1 (it was on long enough to heat up). The bulb that is **OFF and COLD** is switch 3. The insight is using **heat** as a second state beyond on/off.

mcqs.q: The key insight in the 3-bulbs-3-switches puzzle is to use:
options: Heat (a warm bulb) as an extra state
mcqs.explain: Beyond on/off, a bulb's warmth reveals it was recently on, giving a third distinguishable state.

mcqs.q: The bulb that is off but warm corresponds to the switch that was:
options: Turned on for a while then off
mcqs.explain: It was heated by being on, then switched off before you entered.

mcqs.q: The bulb that is off and cold is controlled by the switch that was:
mcqs.explain: An off, cold bulb was never energised — the untouched switch.

u:iv-49-two-ropes-one-hour.title: Two ropes, one hour
u:iv-49-two-ropes-one-hour.summary: Measure 45 minutes with two ropes that each burn unevenly in 60 minutes.

blocks.text: **Puzzle**: Each rope takes exactly 60 minutes to burn but burns **unevenly** (you can't assume half-rope = 30 min). Measure **45 minutes**.

items: Light **rope A at both ends** and **rope B at one end** simultaneously.
Rope A (burning from both ends) finishes in **30 minutes** — regardless of unevenness, two fronts consume the whole rope in half the time.
At that 30-minute mark, rope B has **30 minutes** of burn left. **Light rope B's other end** now.
Rope B's remaining 30 minutes, burning from both ends, finishes in **15 minutes**. Total: 30 + 15 = **45 minutes**.

blocks.text: The trick: **burning from both ends halves the remaining time**, regardless of uneven burn rate. Both-ends of A = 30 min; then both-ends of B's remaining half = 15 min; total 45.

mcqs.q: Burning a 60-minute rope from BOTH ends takes:
mcqs.explain: Two burning fronts consume the whole rope in half the time, regardless of uneven burning.

mcqs.q: To measure 45 minutes, after rope A (both ends) finishes at 30 min you:
options: Light rope B's second end (its remaining 30 min burns in 15)
mcqs.explain: Rope B has 30 min left; lighting its other end finishes it in 15 min, giving 30+15=45.

mcqs.q: The core principle used is that lighting both ends:
mcqs.explain: Regardless of burn unevenness, two fronts halve the time to consume the remaining rope.

u:iv-50-poisoned-wine-bottles.title: Poisoned wine bottles
u:iv-50-poisoned-wine-bottles.summary: Find 1 poisoned bottle among 1000 using only 10 test subjects - binary encoding.

blocks.text: **Puzzle**: 1000 wine bottles, exactly one poisoned (poison kills in 24 hours). With one test window, how many **prisoners/testers** are needed to find the poisoned bottle?
Answer: **10**. Number the bottles 0-999 in **binary** (10 bits, since 2^10 = 1024 > 1000). Assign one prisoner per bit. Prisoner i drinks from every bottle whose i-th bit is 1.

After 24 hours, the set of prisoners who die spells out the poisoned bottle's number in **binary** (a dead prisoner = 1, alive = 0). Since 2^10 = 1024 ≥ 1000, **10 prisoners** uniquely identify any of the 1000 bottles. This is binary encoding: n prisoners test up to 2^n bottles.
General rule: k testers can distinguish up to 2^k bottles in one round.

mcqs.q: The minimum number of testers to find 1 poisoned bottle among 1000 (one test round) is:
mcqs.explain: Binary encoding: 2^10 = 1024 ≥ 1000, so 10 testers uniquely identify the bottle.

mcqs.q: The technique used is:
mcqs.explain: Each bottle's binary index maps to which testers drink it; the pattern of deaths reveals the number.

mcqs.q: With k testers, the maximum number of bottles distinguishable in one round is:
mcqs.explain: Each tester is a bit, so k bits encode 2^k distinct bottle indices.

u:iv-51-2-eggs-100-floors.title: 2 eggs, 100 floors
u:iv-51-2-eggs-100-floors.summary: Find the highest safe floor with 2 eggs in the fewest worst-case drops - answer 14.

blocks.text: **Puzzle**: A building has 100 floors. An egg breaks if dropped from floor ≥ the (unknown) critical floor. With **2 eggs**, minimise the **worst-case** number of drops to find that floor.

Answer: **14 drops**. The trick is to balance the cost so every path has the same worst case. Drop the first egg at floors that **decrease the interval by 1 each time**: floor 14, then 14+13=27, then 27+12=39, ... (steps 14,13,12,...).

Find the smallest n with n(n+1)/2 ≥ 100. That's **n = 14** (14×15/2 = 105 ≥ 100). Drop egg 1 at floor 14; if it breaks, use egg 2 to check floors 1-13 one by one (13 more drops = 14 total). If it survives, next drop at 14+13=27, etc. Every branch costs at most 14.
General formula: for F floors and 2 eggs, minimise n where n(n+1)/2 ≥ F.

mcqs.q: The minimum worst-case number of drops for 2 eggs and 100 floors is:
mcqs.explain: The smallest n with n(n+1)/2 ≥ 100 is 14, giving a balanced worst case of 14 drops.

mcqs.q: The first egg is dropped with intervals that:
mcqs.explain: Decreasing steps keep the worst-case total drops constant across all branches.

mcqs.q: If the first egg breaks at the first drop (floor 14), you then:
options: Use the second egg to check floors 1-13 linearly
mcqs.explain: With one egg left you must go linearly upward from the last safe floor to avoid risk.

u:iv-52-bridge-crossing-in-the-dark.title: Bridge crossing in the dark
u:iv-52-bridge-crossing-in-the-dark.summary: Four people, one torch, cross in minimum 17 minutes - send the two fastest back strategically.

blocks.text: **Puzzle**: Four people cross a bridge at night with **one torch**. At most 2 cross at once, and a pair moves at the **slower** person's speed. Times: 1, 2, 5, 10 minutes. Minimum total time?

items: 1 & 2 cross → **2 min**. 1 returns with torch → **1 min**. (3 total)
5 & 10 cross → **10 min**. 2 returns with torch → **2 min**. (15 total)
1 & 2 cross → **2 min**. **Total = 17 minutes**.

blocks.text: Answer: **17**. The insight: send the **two slowest together** (so their times overlap, not add separately), and use the two **fastest** as torch-bearers to ferry it back. The naive 'fastest escorts everyone' gives 19; pairing the slow ones saves 2.
The tempting wrong answer is 19 (1 escorts each). Pairing 5 and 10 together is the key optimisation.

mcqs.q: The minimum time for the 4 people (1,2,5,10) to cross is:
mcqs.explain: Sending the two slowest (5 and 10) together, ferried by the two fastest, yields 17 minutes.

mcqs.q: The key optimisation is to:
options: Have the fastest escort each person
Send the two slowest across together
mcqs.explain: Pairing the two slowest overlaps their times instead of paying each separately.

mcqs.q: A pair crossing the bridge moves at the:
mcqs.explain: They must stay together, so the pair is limited by the slower person.

u:iv-53-8-balls-one-heavier.title: 8 balls, one heavier
u:iv-53-8-balls-one-heavier.summary: Find the one heavier ball among 8 in just 2 weighings on a balance scale.

blocks.text: **Puzzle**: 8 identical-looking balls; one is slightly **heavier**. Using a balance scale, find it in the minimum number of weighings.

items: **Weighing 1**: put **3 vs 3** (set 2 aside). If they balance, the heavy ball is one of the 2 set aside → weigh those 1 vs 1 to find it (weighing 2).
If one side of 3 is heavier, the heavy ball is among those 3. **Weighing 2**: from those 3, weigh **1 vs 1**. If they balance, it's the third; else the heavier pan holds it.

blocks.text: Answer: **2 weighings**. The trick is splitting into **three groups** (3, 3, 2), not halves — each weighing has three outcomes (left heavy, right heavy, balanced), so it narrows a group of 3 in one step. That's why the answer is 2, not 3.
General: with a balance, n weighings distinguish among up to 3^n items (here 3^2 = 9 ≥ 8).

mcqs.q: The minimum number of weighings to find the heavier ball among 8 is:
mcqs.explain: Splitting into groups of 3-3-2 and using the three-outcome balance finds it in 2 weighings.

mcqs.q: The key idea is to divide the balls into:
mcqs.explain: A balance gives three results, so dividing into thirds narrows the search fastest.

mcqs.q: With a balance scale, n weighings can distinguish up to:
mcqs.explain: Each weighing has three outcomes, so n weighings distinguish 3^n possibilities.

u:iv-54-blue-eyed-islanders.title: Blue-eyed islanders
u:iv-54-blue-eyed-islanders.summary: A famous induction puzzle: after N days, all N blue-eyed islanders leave.

blocks.text: **Puzzle**: On an island, everyone can see others' eye colours but not their own, and no one may discuss it. The rule: anyone who deduces they have blue eyes must leave that night. A visitor announces 'at least one of you has blue eyes.' If there are **N** blue-eyed people, what happens?
Answer: all **N blue-eyed islanders leave on night N**, by **induction**.

items: **N=1**: the lone blue-eyed person sees no other blue eyes, so the announcement means it's them → leaves night 1.
**N=2**: each sees 1 blue-eyed person; if that person doesn't leave night 1, each realises there must be 2 → both leave night 2.
**General**: each blue-eyed person waits N-1 nights; when the others haven't left, they deduce they too are blue-eyed → all N leave on night N.

blocks.text: The puzzle's magic is that a seemingly-known fact ('someone has blue eyes') creates **common knowledge**, enabling an inductive chain. Each blue-eyed islander counts the others and leaves on night N when expected departures don't happen.

mcqs.q: With N blue-eyed islanders, they all leave on:
mcqs.explain: By induction, each waits N-1 nights and all N deduce their eye colour on night N.

mcqs.q: The proof technique for this puzzle is:
options: Mathematical induction on the number of blue-eyed people
mcqs.explain: The base case (N=1) extends inductively: if N-1 would leave on night N-1, N leave on night N.

mcqs.q: The announcement matters because it creates:
options: Common knowledge that enables the inductive deduction
mcqs.explain: Making the fact common knowledge lets everyone reason about what everyone else knows, triggering the chain.

u:iv-55-monty-hall.title: Monty Hall
u:iv-55-monty-hall.summary: Switching doors doubles your winning odds from 1/3 to 2/3 - a probability classic.

blocks.text: **Puzzle**: 3 doors; a car behind one, goats behind the others. You pick a door. The host (who knows) opens a **different** door revealing a goat, then offers to let you **switch**. Should you?
Answer: **Yes, switch** — it wins **2/3** of the time vs 1/3 for staying.

items: Your first pick is right with probability **1/3**, wrong with **2/3**.
The host's reveal gives information: he always opens a goat door from the two you didn't pick.
If your original pick was wrong (2/3 of the time), switching lands on the car. So **switching wins with probability 2/3**.

blocks.text: The counter-intuitive key: the host's choice is **not random** — he knowingly avoids the car. That concentrates the remaining 2/3 probability onto the other unopened door. Switching turns your likely-wrong first guess into a likely-right one.
Intuition check: imagine 100 doors — you pick 1 (1% chance), the host opens 98 goats, and the other door now holds the car 99% of the time.

mcqs.q: In the Monty Hall problem, switching doors wins with probability:
mcqs.explain: Your first pick is right 1/3 of the time, so switching wins the other 2/3.

mcqs.q: Switching works because the host's door reveal is:
options: Deliberate (he always reveals a goat), concentrating probability on the other door
mcqs.explain: The host knowingly avoids the car, shifting the 2/3 probability onto the remaining unopened door.

mcqs.q: The best strategy is to:
mcqs.explain: Switching doubles your winning chance from 1/3 to 2/3.

u:iv-56-river-crossing.title: River crossing
u:iv-56-river-crossing.summary: The wolf, goat, cabbage puzzle - ferry items so nothing forbidden is left alone.

blocks.text: **Puzzle**: A farmer must ferry a **wolf, goat, and cabbage** across a river in a boat that holds only him + one item. Left alone, the wolf eats the goat, and the goat eats the cabbage. How?

items: Take the **goat** across, return alone.
Take the **wolf** across, bring the **goat** back.
Take the **cabbage** across, return alone.
Take the **goat** across. Done — nothing forbidden was ever left alone.

blocks.text: The key insight: the **goat is the conflict** (it's in both forbidden pairs), so it can never be left with either. The trick is being willing to **bring the goat back** — the move people miss. You ferry the goat back and forth to keep the wolf and cabbage safely apart.

mcqs.q: The first item the farmer should take across is the:
mcqs.explain: The goat is involved in both conflicts, so it must be moved first (and managed carefully).

mcqs.q: The clever, easily-missed move in the solution is to:
options: Bring the goat back across after dropping the wolf
Leave the wolf with the goat
mcqs.explain: Temporarily returning the goat keeps the wolf and cabbage from being left with it.

mcqs.q: The goat is central to the puzzle because it:
options: Conflicts with both the wolf and the cabbage
mcqs.explain: The goat appears in both forbidden pairs, so it can never be left with either alone.

u:iv-57-angle-between-clock-hands.title: Angle between clock hands
u:iv-57-angle-between-clock-hands.summary: Use the formula |30H - 5.5M| to find the angle between the hour and minute hands.

blocks.text: **Puzzle/formula**: Find the angle between the hour and minute hands at time H:M.

items: The **minute hand** moves 360/60 = **6 degrees per minute**.
The **hour hand** moves 360/12 = 30 degrees per hour = **0.5 degrees per minute**. So at H:M it's at 30H + 0.5M degrees.
**Angle = |30H − 5.5M|** degrees (take H mod 12). If the result exceeds 180, subtract from 360 for the smaller angle.

blocks.text: Memorise **|30H − 5.5M|**. Example at 3:15: |30·3 − 5.5·15| = |90 − 82.5| = **7.5 degrees** (not 0 — the hour hand has moved past 3). Forgetting the hour hand's drift is the classic mistake.
Take the smaller angle: if |30H − 5.5M| > 180, the answer is 360 minus that value.

mcqs.q: The angle between clock hands at H:M is given by:
mcqs.explain: Hour hand moves 0.5 deg/min (30H+0.5M); minute hand 6M; the difference is |30H - 5.5M|.

mcqs.q: The angle between the hands at 3:15 is:
mcqs.explain: |30*3 - 5.5*15| = |90 - 82.5| = 7.5 degrees; the hour hand has drifted past 3.

mcqs.q: If the formula gives more than 180 degrees, the actual (smaller) angle is:
mcqs.explain: Clock-hand angle is the smaller of the two, so subtract from 360 when it exceeds 180.

u:iv-58-ants-on-a-triangle.title: Ants on a triangle
u:iv-58-ants-on-a-triangle.summary: Three ants on a triangle avoid collision with probability 1/4.

blocks.text: **Puzzle**: Three ants sit on the corners of a triangle. Each independently picks a direction (clockwise or counter-clockwise) and walks along an edge. What's the probability that **none collide**?
Answer: **1/4**. Each ant has 2 choices → 2^3 = 8 equally likely outcomes. Ants avoid collision only if **all go the same way** — all clockwise or all counter-clockwise.

Only **2** of the 8 outcomes are collision-free (all-CW or all-CCW). So P(no collision) = 2/8 = **1/4**. Any mix of directions forces at least two ants onto the same edge toward each other. (Generalises to 2/2^n for n ants on an n-gon.)

mcqs.q: The probability that 3 ants on a triangle don't collide is:
mcqs.explain: Only the 2 all-same-direction outcomes (of 8) avoid collision: 2/8 = 1/4.

mcqs.q: The ants avoid collision only when:
options: All choose the same direction (all CW or all CCW)
mcqs.explain: Any mixed choice puts two ants on the same edge heading toward each other.

mcqs.q: How many of the 8 possible direction-combinations are collision-free?
mcqs.explain: Exactly 2: all clockwise and all counter-clockwise.

u:iv-59-coin-on-a-round-table.title: Coin on a round table
u:iv-59-coin-on-a-round-table.summary: A symmetry-strategy game: the first player wins by placing a coin in the centre.

blocks.text: **Puzzle**: Two players take turns placing identical coins on a round table (no overlaps, coins must stay on the table). The player who can't place a coin loses. Who wins, and how?
Answer: the **first player wins** with a symmetry strategy.

items: Player 1 places the **first coin exactly at the centre**.
Thereafter, Player 1 **mirrors** every move Player 2 makes — placing a coin at the point **diametrically opposite** Player 2's last coin.
By symmetry, if Player 2 has a legal spot, its mirror is also free, so Player 1 always has a move. Player 2 eventually runs out first.

blocks.text: The winning idea is **symmetry**: taking the centre first breaks the symmetry in your favour, then mirroring guarantees you always have a reply. This 'strategy-stealing by symmetry' pattern recurs in many combinatorial games.

mcqs.q: In the coin-on-a-round-table game, the winner is the:
mcqs.explain: The first player wins by taking the centre and then mirroring — a symmetry strategy.

mcqs.q: The first player's winning first move is to place a coin:
mcqs.explain: The centre is the unique point with no distinct mirror, breaking symmetry in the first player's favour.

mcqs.q: After the first move, the first player wins by:
mcqs.explain: Mirroring guarantees a legal reply exists whenever the opponent has one.

u:iv-60-prisoners-and-hats.title: Prisoners and hats
u:iv-60-prisoners-and-hats.summary: Prisoners in a line use parity to save all but (at most) one - the classic hat puzzle.

blocks.text: **Puzzle**: N prisoners stand in a line, each wearing a red or black hat, each seeing only the hats **in front** of them. Starting from the back, each must guess their own hat colour (heard by all). How many can be saved with an agreed strategy?
Answer: at least **N−1** are guaranteed saved; the last one has a 50% chance.

items: The **back prisoner** (sees everyone) announces the **parity** of red hats they see — e.g. says 'red' if the count of red hats ahead is odd, 'black' if even. This sacrifices them (50% chance of being right).
Each subsequent prisoner counts red hats **in front** of them and tracks colours **called out behind** them, then deduces their own hat from the parity.

blocks.text: The trick is **encoding parity**: the first guess broadcasts the parity of red hats, and everyone else uses that plus what they see and hear to deduce their own colour with certainty. Only the first prisoner is at risk — so **N−1 guaranteed** saved.

mcqs.q: In the prisoners-and-hats line puzzle, how many can be guaranteed saved?
mcqs.explain: Everyone except the first prisoner can deduce their hat with certainty using parity.

mcqs.q: The strategy relies on the first prisoner announcing the:
options: Parity (odd/even count) of red hats they see
mcqs.explain: Broadcasting the parity of red hats lets everyone else deduce their own colour.

mcqs.q: The first (back) prisoner's own chance of surviving is:
mcqs.explain: They sacrifice certainty to encode parity, so their own guess is a coin flip.

u:iv-61-mock-1-dsa-only.title: Mock 1 - DSA only
u:iv-61-mock-1-dsa-only.summary: Simulate a coding round: solve out loud, under time, with someone watching.

blocks.text: The first mock focuses purely on **DSA problem-solving under interview conditions** — because solving while watched and talking is a different skill from solving alone.

items: Have a peer/mentor give you **1-2 unseen medium problems**; solve them **out loud** within a time limit.
Practise the flow: **clarify → examples/edge cases → approach + complexity → code → test/dry-run**.
Get feedback on communication, not just correctness — did you explain your thinking?
Use a shared editor / whiteboard like the real thing.

blocks.text: The point of a DSA mock is to rehearse **thinking aloud under time and observation**. Even strong solvers freeze when watched — practising the clarify→approach→code→test flow out loud builds the muscle that matters in real coding rounds.

mcqs.q: The main skill a DSA-only mock builds is:
options: Solving out loud under time and observation
mcqs.explain: Verbalising your approach while watched is a distinct skill from solving alone that mocks develop.

mcqs.q: A good problem-solving flow to rehearse is:
options: Clarify → examples/edge cases → approach + complexity → code → test
mcqs.explain: This structured, communicative flow is what interviewers evaluate.

mcqs.q: Feedback in a DSA mock should cover:
options: Communication and thought process, not just correctness
mcqs.explain: How clearly you reasoned and communicated matters as much as the final answer.

u:iv-62-mock-2-dsa-cs-fundamentals.title: Mock 2 - DSA + CS fundamentals
u:iv-62-mock-2-dsa-cs-fundamentals.summary: Combine a coding problem with rapid-fire core CS questions (OS/DBMS/CN/OOP).

blocks.text: The second mock adds **core CS fundamentals** to DSA, mirroring rounds (common at product and service firms) that mix a coding problem with theory questions.

items: One DSA problem, then **rapid-fire fundamentals**: OS (deadlock, scheduling), DBMS (normalization, ACID, indexing), CN (TCP/IP, DNS), OOP (SOLID, polymorphism).
Practise **concise, confident** answers — 30-60 seconds each, with an example.
Identify weak subjects and drill them.
This tests **breadth** under mild pressure.

blocks.text: This mock reveals whether you can switch between deep problem-solving and crisp fundamentals recall. Aim for concise, example-backed answers to theory questions — rambling or blanking on basics costs offers even when your DSA is strong.

mcqs.q: This mock combines DSA with:
options: Core CS fundamentals (OS, DBMS, CN, OOP)
mcqs.explain: It mirrors rounds mixing a coding problem with rapid-fire theory questions.

mcqs.q: Fundamentals answers should be:
options: Concise and confident, ideally with an example
mcqs.explain: Crisp, example-backed answers demonstrate real understanding under pressure.

mcqs.q: A benefit of this mock is that it:
mcqs.explain: Rapid-fire questions expose gaps in fundamentals so you can target them.

u:iv-63-mock-3-full-technical-round.title: Mock 3 - full technical round
u:iv-63-mock-3-full-technical-round.summary: A complete technical interview: intro, DSA, fundamentals, and follow-ups end to end.

blocks.text: This mock simulates a **complete technical round** end to end — the way a real interviewer would run it — to build stamina and flow across question types.

items: Full arc: brief intro → 1-2 DSA problems with **follow-ups/optimisations** → CS fundamentals → maybe a small design/OOP question.
Practise **handling follow-ups** (‘can you optimise?’, ‘what if input is huge?’) and staying composed when pushed.
Simulate real length (45-60 min) to build endurance.
Debrief on both content and demeanor (nervousness, clarity, recovery from a stumble).

blocks.text: A full-round mock builds **stamina and composure across a real interview arc**, especially handling follow-up pressure ('optimise it', 'what about edge cases'). The goal is to make the real thing feel familiar, not novel.

mcqs.q: The purpose of a full technical-round mock is to:
options: Simulate the complete round to build stamina and flow
mcqs.explain: It rehearses the entire arc end to end so the real interview feels familiar.

mcqs.q: A key skill to practise here is:
options: Handling follow-up questions and pressure to optimise
mcqs.explain: Interviewers push with follow-ups; staying composed and improving your solution is vital.

mcqs.q: The debrief should cover:
options: Both content and demeanor (clarity, composure, recovery)
mcqs.explain: How you carry yourself and recover from stumbles matters alongside the technical content.

u:iv-64-mock-4-project-deep-dive.title: Mock 4 - project deep dive
u:iv-64-mock-4-project-deep-dive.summary: Defend a project end to end: architecture, decisions, trade-offs, and what you'd change.

blocks.text: This mock drills **defending your projects** — interviewers probe your resume projects deeply, and vague answers here sink otherwise-strong candidates.

items: Have someone grill you on a project: **architecture, why this stack, the hardest bug, trade-offs, what you'd change, how it scales**.
Practise **drawing the architecture from memory** and explaining each component.
Prepare a crisp **90-second pitch** plus depth on demand.
Only claim what you genuinely did; be honest about team contributions.

blocks.text: Projects are where interviewers verify you can actually build — so rehearse explaining architecture, justifying decisions, and answering 'what would you change?'. Being able to draw and defend your project from memory separates real builders from resume-padders.

mcqs.q: In a project deep-dive, you should be ready to explain:
options: Architecture, decisions, trade-offs, and what you'd change
mcqs.explain: Interviewers probe design decisions and trade-offs to verify genuine understanding.

mcqs.q: A strong preparation is to:
options: Practise drawing the architecture from memory and defending each part
mcqs.explain: Being able to diagram and justify the design from memory demonstrates real ownership.

mcqs.q: You should claim on your resume only projects you:
options: Genuinely contributed to and can defend in depth
mcqs.explain: Deep probing exposes exaggeration, so only claim work you truly did and understand.

u:iv-65-mock-5-hr-behavioural.title: Mock 5 - HR + behavioural
u:iv-65-mock-5-hr-behavioural.summary: Rehearse behavioural answers aloud and timed - written prep doesn't transfer to speech.

blocks.text: This mock rehearses **HR and behavioural** questions **out loud**, because written answers don't transfer to natural speech — you need to have said them before.

items: Have someone ask the standard set: tell me about yourself, why us, strengths/weaknesses, conflict/failure STAR stories.
Deliver each **aloud and timed** — aim for natural, not memorised-robotic.
Get feedback on **body language, filler words, and confidence**, not just content.
Refine your **STAR stories** so they're concise and land the point.

blocks.text: Behavioural answers must be **spoken, not just written** — saying your STAR stories aloud beforehand is what makes them fluent and confident in the real interview. Practise for natural delivery (no rambling, no robotic recitation).

mcqs.q: The most important reason to mock HR questions out loud is that:
options: Spoken delivery differs from written prep and needs rehearsal
mcqs.explain: Answers you've only written often come out awkwardly; speaking them builds fluency and confidence.

mcqs.q: Feedback in an HR mock should include:
options: Delivery: body language, filler words, and confidence too
mcqs.explain: How you come across matters in behavioural rounds, not just what you say.

mcqs.q: Your STAR stories should be:
options: Concise and rehearsed to land the point
mcqs.explain: Tight, practised STAR stories deliver clear impact under pressure.

u:iv-66-mock-6-full-loop-simulation.title: Mock 6 - full loop simulation
u:iv-66-mock-6-full-loop-simulation.summary: Back-to-back rounds in one sitting to build the endurance a real interview day needs.

blocks.text: This mock simulates a **full interview loop** — several rounds back to back in one day — to build the **endurance and consistency** real on-site/virtual loops demand.

items: Run **3-4 rounds in a row**: e.g. DSA, DSA + design, fundamentals, and HR — with short breaks like a real day.
Goal: stay **sharp and consistent** across rounds; fatigue and one bad round often sink candidates.
Practise **resetting** after a rough round so it doesn't cascade.
Debrief on stamina, consistency, and energy management.

blocks.text: Real loops are a marathon: a full-loop mock trains **endurance and the ability to reset after a weak round**. Many capable candidates fail not on any single question but on fading or spiralling across a long day — practise the whole sequence.

mcqs.q: A full-loop simulation primarily builds:
options: Endurance and consistency across multiple back-to-back rounds
mcqs.explain: It rehearses staying sharp across a long, multi-round interview day.

mcqs.q: A key skill to practise between rounds is:
options: Giving up after a bad round
Resetting so one weak round doesn't cascade
mcqs.explain: Recovering mentally after a rough round prevents a downward spiral across the loop.

mcqs.q: Many strong candidates fail a loop due to:
options: Fatigue or spiralling across the day, not a single question
mcqs.explain: Endurance and emotional consistency across rounds often decide outcomes.

u:iv-67-mock-7-company-specific-pattern.title: Mock 7 - company-specific pattern
u:iv-67-mock-7-company-specific-pattern.summary: Tailor a mock to your target company's known format and question style.

blocks.text: This mock is **tailored to a specific target company's pattern** — since Amazon (LP-based), Google (hard DSA), service firms (aptitude + basics), etc. differ significantly.

items: **Research** the company's process (rounds, difficulty, focus) and replicate it.
For Amazon: **Leadership-Principle behavioural** + DSA; for Google: **optimal DSA** with heavy communication; for service firms: **aptitude + fundamentals + basic coding**.
Use company-tagged problems and past-experience reports.
Practise the **specific format** you'll actually face.

blocks.text: Generic prep isn't enough for your top choice — replicate that company's actual pattern (question style, difficulty, behavioural framework). A mock matching the real format removes surprises and lets you rehearse exactly what's coming.

mcqs.q: A company-specific mock should replicate the target's:
options: Actual round structure, difficulty, and focus
mcqs.explain: Matching the real pattern removes surprises and rehearses exactly what you'll face.

mcqs.q: For an Amazon-specific mock, you'd emphasise:
mcqs.explain: Amazon's process is LP-driven behavioural plus coding, so a mock should reflect that.

mcqs.q: For a service-based company mock, focus on:
mcqs.explain: Service firms emphasise aptitude and fundamentals with basic coding, not advanced DSA.

u:iv-68-mock-8-final-dress-rehearsal.title: Mock 8 - final dress rehearsal
u:iv-68-mock-8-final-dress-rehearsal.summary: A full realistic run-through right before the real thing - polish, don't cram.

blocks.text: The final mock is a **dress rehearsal** close to the real interview: full setup, professional demeanor, realistic conditions — to arrive confident, not cramming.

items: Do a **complete, realistic run** (video on, professional attire if virtual, quiet setup, real timing).
Focus on **polish and confidence**, not learning new material — last-minute cramming raises anxiety.
Check logistics: **tech setup, quiet environment, water, resume/portfolio links ready**.
End on a **confidence-building** note; trust your preparation.

blocks.text: The dress rehearsal is about **polish and mindset**, not new content. Simulate the real conditions (setup, attire, timing) so nothing on the day is unfamiliar, and go in calm and confident. Cramming now hurts more than it helps.

mcqs.q: The final dress-rehearsal mock should focus on:
mcqs.explain: Right before the interview, refine delivery and mindset rather than absorbing new material.

mcqs.q: Part of a dress rehearsal is checking:
options: Logistics: tech setup, environment, and having resume/links ready
mcqs.explain: Verifying the real-day setup prevents technical or environmental surprises.

mcqs.q: Last-minute cramming before an interview tends to:
options: Raise anxiety and hurt more than help
mcqs.explain: By this point, calm confidence beats frantic cramming, which increases stress.

u:iv-22-one-page-ats-safe-formatting.title: One page, ATS-safe formatting
u:iv-22-one-page-ats-safe-formatting.summary: A clean, single-page, parseable resume that survives automated screening.

blocks.text: Most large companies run resumes through an **ATS (Applicant Tracking System)** before a human sees them. A poorly formatted resume can be auto-rejected regardless of your skills.

items: **One page** for students/freshers — recruiters skim for seconds.
**Simple, single-column layout**, standard fonts, no images/graphics/tables/columns that ATS can't parse.
**Standard section headings** (Experience, Education, Projects, Skills) so the ATS maps them correctly.
Include **keywords from the job description** naturally, since ATS filters on them. Export as **PDF** (unless they ask for .docx).

blocks.text: Keep it one page, single-column, plain fonts, standard headings, and keyword-aligned to the job — so both the ATS and a skimming recruiter can parse it in seconds. Fancy templates with graphics often break ATS parsing.

mcqs.q: Why should a fresher's resume avoid images, tables, and multi-column layouts?
options: ATS software often can't parse them, risking auto-rejection
mcqs.explain: Applicant Tracking Systems parse text; complex layouts can garble or drop content, causing rejection.

mcqs.q: The ideal resume length for a student/fresher is:
mcqs.explain: One page is standard for early-career candidates; recruiters skim briefly.

mcqs.q: To pass ATS keyword filters, you should:
options: Naturally include relevant keywords from the job description
mcqs.explain: ATS matches on role-relevant keywords, so mirror the job description's language honestly.

u:iv-23-bullets-quantified-impact-not-du.title: Bullets quantified - impact, not duties
u:iv-23-bullets-quantified-impact-not-du.summary: Write achievement bullets with action verbs and numbers, not job-description duties.

blocks.text: Weak resumes list **responsibilities** ('was responsible for the backend'); strong resumes show **impact** ('built an API that cut response time 40%'). Quantify wherever possible.
The formula
**Action verb + what you did + quantified result.** e.g. 'Optimised DB queries, reducing page load from 3s to 0.8s' or 'Led a 4-person team to ship X, used by 500+ students.'

items: Start each bullet with a strong **action verb** (Built, Designed, Reduced, Automated, Led).
Add **numbers**: %, time saved, users, scale — even estimates.
Focus on **outcomes** you drove, not the task description.

blocks.text: Impact + numbers beats duties every time. 'Action verb → what → quantified result' turns a vague task into evidence of value. Recruiters remember 'cut load time 40%', not 'worked on performance'.

mcqs.q: The strongest resume bullet format is:
options: Action verb + what you did + quantified result
mcqs.explain: Quantified, action-led bullets show impact, which is far more compelling than listing duties.

mcqs.q: Which bullet is best?
options: 'Rebuilt the checkout flow, reducing cart abandonment by 25%'
mcqs.explain: It uses an action verb and a quantified outcome, demonstrating real impact.

mcqs.q: Quantifying bullets matters because numbers:
mcqs.explain: Metrics turn claims into evidence and stick in a recruiter's memory.

u:iv-24-projects-section-with-live-links.title: Projects section with live links
u:iv-24-projects-section-with-live-links.summary: Showcase real, working projects with links so reviewers can verify your work.

blocks.text: For freshers, the **projects section is often the most important** — it's your proof of ability when you lack work experience. Make it verifiable.

items: Include a **live demo link** and/or **GitHub repo** for each project — reviewers value proof they can click.
For each: a one-line description, the **tech stack**, and your **specific contribution** (especially in team projects).
Pick projects that show **breadth and depth** relevant to the role; quality over quantity (2-3 strong beats 6 weak).
Ensure links actually work and repos are public with real code.

blocks.text: Working links (demo + GitHub) turn claims into verifiable proof. For freshers, well-chosen, functioning projects with clear tech stacks and your role stated are often the deciding factor — more than coursework.
A dead demo link or an empty/broken repo is worse than no link — always test them before applying.

mcqs.q: For freshers, the projects section is important because it:
options: Provides verifiable proof of ability when work experience is limited
mcqs.explain: Projects demonstrate real skills, standing in for professional experience.

mcqs.q: Each project should ideally include:
options: A live/repo link, tech stack, and your specific contribution
mcqs.explain: Links and clear details let reviewers verify the work and understand your role.

mcqs.q: A broken demo link or empty repo is:
options: Worse than no link — always verify links work
mcqs.explain: A dead link undermines credibility; test everything before submitting.

u:iv-25-skills-section-honest-to-what-yo.title: Skills section honest to what you can defend
u:iv-25-skills-section-honest-to-what-yo.summary: List only skills you can be interviewed on — every item is fair game.

blocks.text: Interviewers probe anything on your resume. Listing a skill you can't back up is a **fast way to lose credibility** mid-interview.

items: Only list skills you can **discuss and be tested on** — if you put 'React', expect React questions.
Consider grouping by proficiency or category (Languages, Frameworks, Tools) rather than one long unranked list.
Avoid buzzword-stuffing ('expert in 20 technologies') — it invites tough questions and reads as inflated.
It's fine to list a skill you're learning if you're honest about your level when asked.

blocks.text: Everything on your resume is interview fair game. List only what you can defend — one skill you know well beats five you half-know, because a single failed probe on an inflated claim damages trust in the whole resume.

mcqs.q: You should list a skill on your resume only if you:
options: Can discuss and be interviewed on it
Saw it in the job description
mcqs.explain: Interviewers test listed skills; unable-to-defend claims quickly destroy credibility.

mcqs.q: Buzzword-stuffing the skills section:
options: Invites tough questions and reads as inflated/dishonest
mcqs.explain: Overclaiming skills backfires when probed and undermines trust in your whole resume.

mcqs.q: The consequence of listing an unfamiliar skill is:
options: A failed probe that damages trust in the entire resume
mcqs.explain: One caught exaggeration makes interviewers doubt everything else you claimed.

u:iv-26-linkedin-headline-and-about-rewr.title: LinkedIn headline and About rewritten
u:iv-26-linkedin-headline-and-about-rewr.summary: A specific headline and a real About section make recruiters reach out.

blocks.text: Recruiters search LinkedIn heavily. A strong **headline** and **About** section improve discoverability and first impression.

items: **Headline**: more than 'Student at X' — say what you do and target, e.g. 'CS Undergrad | Backend & DSA | Java, Node' (keywords help search).
**About**: a short first-person summary of who you are, your focus/strengths, and what you're seeking — not a wall of buzzwords.
Fill out experience, projects, and skills; keep it consistent with your resume.
A professional photo and complete profile raise credibility and search ranking.

blocks.text: Optimise the headline with role-relevant keywords (recruiters search them) and write a genuine, concise About that states your focus and what you want. A complete, keyword-rich profile gets you found and messaged.

mcqs.q: A strong LinkedIn headline is:
options: Specific and keyword-rich, e.g. 'CS Undergrad | Backend | Java, Node'
mcqs.explain: Specific keywords improve recruiter search discoverability and convey your focus.

mcqs.q: The About section should be:
options: A concise, genuine summary of your focus, strengths, and goals
A copy of your entire resume
mcqs.explain: A readable, authentic summary makes a good first impression and aids search.

mcqs.q: Recruiters find candidates on LinkedIn primarily by:
mcqs.explain: Keyword search is central, so a keyword-optimised, complete profile ranks higher and gets contacted.

u:iv-27-github-pinned-repos-with-real-re.title: GitHub pinned repos with real READMEs
u:iv-27-github-pinned-repos-with-real-re.summary: Curate pinned repos and write READMEs that explain and demo each project.

blocks.text: Interviewers and recruiters look at your GitHub. **Pinned repos with good READMEs** turn it into a portfolio; an empty or messy profile undersells you.

items: **Pin your best 3-6 repos** so they appear first — quality curation, not every experiment.
Each repo needs a **README**: what it does, how to run it, tech stack, a screenshot/demo GIF or link.
Clean commit history and clear structure signal professionalism.
Remove or hide half-finished, embarrassing repos from the pinned view.

blocks.text: A good README is what makes a repo valuable to a reviewer — it explains and demonstrates the project so they don't have to read all the code. Pin your strongest work and let the READMEs sell it.

mcqs.q: Pinned GitHub repos should be:
options: Your best 3-6, curated to appear first
mcqs.explain: Curating your strongest work up front makes the best impression.

mcqs.q: A good repo README includes:
options: What it does, how to run it, tech stack, and a demo/screenshot
mcqs.explain: A clear README lets reviewers understand and try the project without reading all the code.

mcqs.q: A GitHub profile matters because interviewers:
options: Often review it as a portfolio of your real work
mcqs.explain: Recruiters and interviewers inspect GitHub as evidence of your actual coding.

u:iv-28-leetcode-gfg-profile-made-public.title: LeetCode / GFG profile made public
u:iv-28-leetcode-gfg-profile-made-public.summary: A visible problem-solving profile signals consistent DSA practice.

blocks.text: A public **LeetCode / GeeksforGeeks / Codeforces** profile is tangible proof of your **DSA practice and consistency** — valued for product-based roles.

items: Make the profile **public** and link it on your resume/LinkedIn if the numbers are respectable.
It shows **volume, difficulty spread, and consistency** (streaks, contest ratings) — proof you practice, not just claim.
Only showcase it if it's reasonably strong; a sparse profile is better left unlinked.

blocks.text: A visible competitive-programming/DSA profile is credible evidence of consistent practice — a plus for product-company applications. Link it when the record supports you; skip it if it's thin.

mcqs.q: A public LeetCode/GFG profile primarily signals:
mcqs.explain: It provides visible proof of coding-problem practice, valued for product roles.

mcqs.q: You should link your competitive-programming profile when it is:
mcqs.explain: Showcase it only if the record helps you; a sparse profile can hurt more than help.

mcqs.q: Such profiles are most valued by:
mcqs.explain: Product companies weigh DSA heavily, so a strong problem-solving profile is a plus there.

u:iv-29-portfolio-site-live.title: Portfolio site live
u:iv-29-portfolio-site-live.summary: A simple personal site aggregates your work and doubles as a project itself.

blocks.text: A **live portfolio website** presents your projects, skills, and contact in one place — and building/deploying it is itself a small project that demonstrates full-stack ability.

items: Keep it **simple and fast**: about, projects (with links), skills, resume download, contact.
**Deploy it** (Netlify/Vercel/GitHub Pages) with a clean custom domain if possible.
It shows initiative and that you can ship and deploy something real.
Link it from your resume and LinkedIn.

blocks.text: A live, deployed portfolio is a two-for-one: it aggregates your work in one clickable place AND proves you can build and ship. Keep it clean and functional — a broken or over-designed site backfires.

mcqs.q: A portfolio site provides a double benefit because it:
options: Aggregates your work AND demonstrates you can build/deploy something
mcqs.explain: It both showcases projects and serves as evidence of shipping a real, deployed product.

mcqs.q: A portfolio site should be:
mcqs.explain: A clean, functional, live site makes the best impression; a broken one hurts.

mcqs.q: Where should you link your portfolio?
mcqs.explain: Linking it from your resume and LinkedIn maximises visibility to recruiters.

u:iv-30-reviewed-by-two-other-people.title: Reviewed by two other people
u:iv-30-reviewed-by-two-other-people.summary: Fresh eyes catch typos, weak bullets, and unclear points you've gone blind to.

blocks.text: After many edits you stop seeing your own resume's flaws. Having **2+ people review** it catches errors and improves clarity before recruiters see it.

items: Ask a **peer/senior** (ideally in tech) and someone detail-oriented to review.
They catch **typos, grammar, unclear bullets, and formatting issues** you've become blind to.
A senior can flag if your bullets convey impact and if the level/keywords fit your target roles.
One typo can cost an interview at competitive companies — reviews are cheap insurance.

blocks.text: Never send a resume only you have read. Two reviewers — one for detail (typos/clarity) and one senior (impact/fit) — catch what you can't see anymore. It's the cheapest quality boost available.

mcqs.q: Getting your resume reviewed by others helps because:
options: Fresh eyes catch errors and unclear points you've gone blind to
mcqs.explain: After many edits you miss your own flaws; others spot typos, weak bullets, and clarity issues.

mcqs.q: Ideal reviewers include:
options: A detail-oriented person and a tech senior
mcqs.explain: Detail review catches errors; a senior assesses impact and role fit.

mcqs.q: A single typo on a resume can:
options: Cost an interview at competitive companies
mcqs.explain: Small errors signal carelessness and can eliminate you when competition is high.

u:iv-31-separate-variant-for-product-vs-.title: Separate variant for product vs service roles
u:iv-31-separate-variant-for-product-vs-.summary: Tailor two resume versions — DSA/projects for product, breadth/aptitude for service.

blocks.text: Product-based (FAANG-style) and service-based (TCS/Infosys-style) companies value different things. A **tailored variant** for each converts better than one generic resume.

rows: DSA, strong projects, system/design exposure, CP profile
Breadth, adaptability, communication, core CS, willingness to learn
Reliable generalist, good fit for training

blocks.text: Tailoring beats generic: for product roles lead with DSA depth and impactful projects; for service roles emphasise breadth, adaptability, and communication. Keep the same true content — just reorder/emphasise to match what each values.
This is reprioritising, not fabricating — every version must be honest. You're highlighting the parts most relevant to each employer type.

mcqs.q: Product-based companies' resumes should emphasise:
options: DSA, strong projects, and technical depth
mcqs.explain: Product companies weigh algorithmic depth and impactful projects heavily.

mcqs.q: Service-based company resumes benefit from emphasising:
options: Breadth, adaptability, communication, and core fundamentals
mcqs.explain: Service companies value versatile, trainable generalists with good communication.

mcqs.q: Tailoring resume variants means:
options: Honestly reordering/emphasising relevant content for each employer type
mcqs.explain: You highlight the most relevant true content for each audience, never fabricate.

u:iv-32-tcs-nqt-sections-timing-cutoffs.title: TCS NQT - sections, timing, cutoffs
u:iv-32-tcs-nqt-sections-timing-cutoffs.summary: A structured aptitude + coding test; know the sections and manage time per section.

blocks.text: The **TCS National Qualifier Test (NQT)** is a common gateway for TCS (and shared with other firms). It's a structured, sectional, often time-bound-per-section online test.

items: Typical sections: **Numerical Ability (quant)**, **Verbal Ability**, **Reasoning Ability**, and a **Programming/Coding** section (a couple of coding problems).
Sections are usually **individually timed** — you can't borrow time across them, so pace each.
There may be **sectional cutoffs** (clear each section) plus an overall cutoff.
Preparation focus: aptitude practice + basic coding (arrays, strings, simple logic). Speed and accuracy both matter.

blocks.text: The structure to internalise: sectional timing (pace each section, don't overspend on one) and possible sectional cutoffs (you must clear each, not just the total). Balanced prep across aptitude + basic coding is key.

mcqs.q: The TCS NQT typically has:
options: Multiple sections (numerical, verbal, reasoning, programming), often individually timed
mcqs.explain: It's a sectional aptitude + coding test, usually with per-section timing.

mcqs.q: Sections being individually timed means you should:
options: Pace each section since time can't be borrowed across them
Do them in any order without limits
mcqs.explain: Per-section timers require managing time within each section separately.

mcqs.q: Sectional cutoffs require you to:
mcqs.explain: You must clear each section's threshold, not just the aggregate.

u:iv-33-tcs-digital-advanced-pattern.title: TCS Digital - advanced pattern
u:iv-33-tcs-digital-advanced-pattern.summary: A higher-package track with tougher coding and a more technical interview.

blocks.text: **TCS Digital** is a higher-compensation offer track (above the base Ninja/entry role), reached via a higher NQT score and/or a tougher test, with more technical interviews.

items: Requires clearing a **higher cutoff** and typically harder **coding** than the base track.
Interviews are more **technical**: deeper DSA, projects, and CS fundamentals (OOP, DBMS, OS, CN).
Sometimes an **Advanced Coding** section separates Digital candidates from the base pool.
Prep like a mid-tier product role: solid DSA + strong core CS + defensible projects.

blocks.text: TCS Digital = the higher-package variant: reached by a higher score/harder coding, with more technical interviews. Treat it as a step up from Ninja — stronger DSA and core CS depth are what separate Digital candidates.

mcqs.q: TCS Digital differs from the base TCS track by:
options: Offering a higher package with a tougher test and more technical interviews
mcqs.explain: Digital is the higher-compensation track reached via higher performance and harder rounds.

mcqs.q: To reach TCS Digital you typically need:
options: A higher NQT score / advanced coding performance
mcqs.explain: A higher cutoff and stronger coding separate Digital candidates from the base pool.

mcqs.q: Digital interviews emphasise:
options: Deeper DSA, projects, and core CS fundamentals
mcqs.explain: The technical bar is higher — solid DSA and core CS depth are expected.

u:iv-34-infosys-sp-dse-pattern.title: Infosys - SP/DSE pattern
u:iv-34-infosys-sp-dse-pattern.summary: Higher-package Infosys tracks (System/Specialist Programmer, DSE) with harder coding.

blocks.text: Infosys hires across tiers: the base **Systems Engineer (SE)**, and higher tracks like **Specialist/System Programmer (SP)** and **Digital Specialist Engineer (DSE)** with better packages and harder tests.

items: Base SE: aptitude + basic technical; higher tracks (SP/DSE) require stronger **coding/DSA** and a more technical interview.
SP/DSE cutoffs and coding difficulty are notably higher than the base role.
Prep: aptitude + pseudocode/coding basics for SE; solid DSA + core CS for SP/DSE.

blocks.text: Infosys has tiers: base SE (aptitude + basics) up to SP/DSE (harder coding, better pay, more technical interview). Target the higher tracks with real DSA and core CS depth, not just aptitude.

mcqs.q: Infosys's higher tracks (SP/DSE) compared to the base SE role require:
options: Stronger coding/DSA and a more technical interview for a better package
mcqs.explain: SP/DSE are higher-compensation tracks with harder coding and technical bars than base SE.

mcqs.q: For the base Infosys Systems Engineer role, prep focuses on:
mcqs.explain: The base track emphasises aptitude and fundamental coding, with higher tracks adding DSA depth.

mcqs.q: DSE (Digital Specialist Engineer) is:
options: A higher-package specialist track with a tougher process
mcqs.explain: DSE is among the higher Infosys tracks, requiring stronger technical performance.

u:iv-35-wipro-elite-turbo.title: Wipro Elite / Turbo
u:iv-35-wipro-elite-turbo.summary: Wipro's standard (Elite NTH) and higher-package (Turbo) hiring tracks.

blocks.text: **Wipro Elite (NTH - National Talent Hunt)** is the standard entry hiring; **Wipro Turbo** is a higher-package track for stronger candidates, typically with tougher assessment.

items: **Elite**: an online test (aptitude, verbal, logical, basic coding) + essay/written English + interviews.
**Turbo**: higher cutoff and more challenging coding/technical rounds for a better package.
Wipro often includes a **written communication (essay)** section — don't neglect it.
Prep: aptitude + basic coding for Elite; add DSA depth for Turbo.

blocks.text: Wipro Elite (standard) vs Turbo (higher package, harder test) — the same tier pattern as TCS/Infosys. Note Wipro's essay/written-English component, which some candidates overlook.

mcqs.q: Wipro Turbo differs from Elite by:
options: Offering a higher package via a tougher assessment
mcqs.explain: Turbo is the higher-compensation track requiring stronger performance than standard Elite.

mcqs.q: A component of Wipro's hiring some candidates overlook is:
mcqs.explain: Wipro often assesses written English via an essay, which shouldn't be neglected.

mcqs.q: The Elite (NTH) test covers:
options: Aptitude, verbal, logical, and basic coding
mcqs.explain: The standard test spans aptitude, verbal/logical reasoning, and basic coding.

u:iv-36-accenture.title: Accenture
u:iv-36-accenture.summary: A mass-recruiter process: cognitive + technical assessment, coding, and communication.

blocks.text: **Accenture** is a large mass recruiter with a multi-stage assessment emphasising aptitude, basic technical knowledge, coding, and communication.

items: Typical stages: **Cognitive assessment** (aptitude, verbal, reasoning), **Technical assessment** (fundamentals: networking, cloud, common apps, pseudocode), a **coding round** (2 problems), and a **communication assessment**.
A distinctive **Communication Assessment** (spoken English) is part of the process — practise it.
Prep: aptitude + basic tech fundamentals + simple coding; polish spoken English.

blocks.text: Accenture's process is aptitude-heavy with basic technical + coding and a notable spoken-communication assessment. Prepare broadly (aptitude, fundamentals, simple coding) and practise speaking clearly for the communication round.

mcqs.q: A distinctive stage in Accenture's process is the:
mcqs.explain: Accenture includes a spoken communication assessment alongside cognitive/technical stages.

mcqs.q: Accenture's assessment is best described as:
options: Aptitude-heavy with basic technical fundamentals and simple coding
mcqs.explain: It emphasises aptitude and fundamentals with a basic coding round, not advanced algorithms.

mcqs.q: As a mass recruiter, Accenture prioritises candidates who are:
mcqs.explain: Broad competence and communication fit its large-scale, generalist hiring.

u:iv-37-cognizant-genc.title: Cognizant GenC
u:iv-37-cognizant-genc.summary: Cognizant's tiered GenC / GenC Next / GenC Elevate tracks with rising difficulty.

blocks.text: **Cognizant** hires through **GenC** and higher tiers like **GenC Next** and **GenC Elevate**, with increasing package and difficulty.

items: **GenC**: aptitude + basic coding + technical + communication — the standard track.
**GenC Next / Elevate**: higher packages requiring stronger **DSA/coding** and more technical interviews.
Assessment spans aptitude, reasoning, and coding; higher tiers weight coding more.
Prep: aptitude + basic coding for GenC; solid DSA + core CS for the elevated tiers.

blocks.text: Same tier pattern again: GenC (standard) → GenC Next/Elevate (higher pay, harder coding). Aim higher by building real DSA and core CS strength beyond aptitude.

mcqs.q: Cognizant's higher tiers (GenC Next/Elevate) compared to base GenC require:
options: Stronger DSA/coding for a higher package

u:iv-39-deloitte.summary: A consulting-firm process weighing communication, assessments, and fit alongside tech.

blocks.text: **Deloitte** (a consulting/services firm) hiring often includes online assessments, versant/communication tests, and interviews that weigh **communication, aptitude, and behavioural fit** alongside technical basics.

items: Online assessment (aptitude, verbal, sometimes technical MCQs) and a **communication/versant** test.

u:iv-40-amazon-oa-2-problems-workstyles.title: Amazon OA - 2 problems + workstyles
u:iv-40-amazon-oa-2-problems-workstyles.summary: Amazon's online assessment: two DSA problems plus a Leadership Principles work-style survey.

items: **Two DSA problems** — usually medium difficulty (arrays, strings, graphs, DP, etc.); correctness + passing test cases matters.

blocks.text: Amazon is uniquely **Leadership-Principles-driven**: the OA has 2 DSA problems AND a work-styles survey, and interviews mix DSA with LP-based behavioural questions. Prepare STAR stories tagged to specific principles (Ownership, Customer Obsession, etc.).

u:iv-41-microsoft.title: Microsoft
u:iv-41-microsoft.summary: A product-company loop: multiple DSA rounds plus design and a culture-fit round.

blocks.text: **Microsoft** runs a product-company interview loop: an online coding assessment (for campus), then multiple **DSA-focused interviews**, some design, and a final culture/fit round (often 'AA' - As Appropriate).

items: **Strong DSA** across rounds: trees, graphs, DP, strings — with clean code and clear communication of your approach.
Some rounds include **design/OOP** or problem-solving discussion; senior interviewers probe depth.
**Culture fit / behavioural** matters (growth mindset is a Microsoft value).
Prep: DSA depth + articulate problem-solving + core CS + a couple of behavioural stories.

blocks.text: Microsoft is DSA-heavy across several rounds with clear communication expected, plus design/OOP and a culture-fit round. Practise solving out loud with clean code — how you reason matters as much as the answer.

mcqs.q: Microsoft's interview loop is primarily:
options: Multiple DSA-focused rounds plus design and culture fit
mcqs.explain: It's a product-company loop emphasising DSA, with design and a culture/fit round.

mcqs.q: Beyond correctness, Microsoft interviewers value:
options: Clear communication of your approach and clean code
mcqs.explain: Articulating your reasoning and writing clean code weighs heavily in the evaluation.

mcqs.q: A Microsoft cultural value to reflect is:
mcqs.explain: Microsoft emphasises a growth mindset, worth demonstrating in behavioural answers.

u:iv-42-google.title: Google
u:iv-42-google.summary: Multiple deep DSA rounds emphasising optimal solutions, edge cases, and clarity.

blocks.text: **Google's** process is famously **DSA-heavy**: several coding rounds demanding **optimal solutions**, strong analysis, and clean communication, plus 'Googleyness'/behavioural.

items: Expect **hard problem-solving**: graphs, DP, trees, complex data structures — with attention to **time/space complexity** and **edge cases**.
Interviewers value your **thought process**: clarify the problem, discuss approaches/trade-offs, then code cleanly and test.
**Googleyness & Leadership** round assesses collaboration, humility, and culture.
Prep: deep DSA (LeetCode medium/hard), complexity analysis, and clear out-loud problem solving.

blocks.text: Google demands optimal solutions and rigorous reasoning, not just a working answer: clarify, discuss trade-offs, analyse complexity, handle edge cases, and communicate throughout. Depth of problem-solving and clarity are the bar.

mcqs.q: Google's coding rounds especially emphasise:
options: Optimal solutions with complexity analysis and edge cases
mcqs.explain: Google expects optimal, well-analysed solutions and rigorous handling of edge cases.

mcqs.explain: Communicating your reasoning and trade-offs is central to the evaluation.

mcqs.q: The 'Googleyness & Leadership' round assesses:

u:iv-43-adobe.title: Adobe
u:iv-43-adobe.summary: DSA plus a strong emphasis on core CS (OS/DBMS/OOP) and project depth.

blocks.text: **Adobe's** process combines **DSA** with a notable emphasis on **core CS fundamentals** (OS, DBMS, OOP, sometimes CN) and deep discussion of your **projects**.

items: An online round (DSA + sometimes aptitude/CS MCQs), then technical interviews.
Interviews probe **DSA + core CS** more than some product firms — be solid on OOP, DBMS, OS.
Expect **project deep-dives**: design decisions, trade-offs, and what you'd improve.
Prep: DSA + strong core CS + defensible projects.

blocks.text: Adobe balances DSA with strong **core CS** (OS/DBMS/OOP) and project depth — don't neglect fundamentals for pure algorithms. Know your projects cold and be ready to justify design decisions.

mcqs.q: Compared to some product firms, Adobe places notable emphasis on:

u:iv-44-goldman-sachs-jpmorgan.title: Goldman Sachs / JPMorgan

items: Online assessment often includes **coding + aptitude/analytical/quant** sections (GS has a well-known multi-part HackerRank test).

blocks.text: Finance-tech firms like GS/JPMorgan blend DSA with **quantitative/analytical aptitude** and core CS — so don't drop aptitude for pure coding. GS's multi-section online test is notable; balanced prep across coding + quant + fundamentals wins.

items: Online coding assessment (DSA), then technical interviews on **DSA + core CS**.
